At the beginning of the video, a drawing of a Chinese warrior preparing a rocket sits in the center of the screen. This drawing appears against an out-of-focus background of a highway. The narrator lists the three components of gunpowder: saltpeter, sulfur, and coal. After that, the video transitions to an out-of-focus shot of a highway in the countryside, then displays an image of Mount Karnasurta, which has slabs of basalt with perfectly even faces. Next, the camera shows a shot of stone scraps at Mount Karnasurta and poses the question: “Do you think these are traces of ancient civilizations?" Finally, the video reveals a final image of stones at Karnasurta and adds, “Scientists think it's a natural formation.” Text reading "Anyway, three ingredients are needed to make gunpowder: saltpeter, sulfur and coal. There has always been coal in China. Until the 18th century, native sulphur was only available at the mouth of the volcano Etna, in Sicily. The nearest deposit of saltpeter was on the island of Ceylon. Of the entire Mendeleev Table, only saltpeter and sulfur can be components of black powder, all other fast-acting substances are explosive, and any cannon would be blown to pieces if used. How could China invent gunpowder with only 1 of 3 components?” The video also displays the web addresses “@Insidemeiseverything and “bitchute.com/eim.” Numbered annotations appear on screen, showing "4 https://t.me/taboo_science1" and "5 https://t.me/taboo_science1" respectively.

Many people would think they were camels, but they weren't." The result was not only a cultural but also historical sensation- on the wall was a small stone bas-relief with the image of stegosaurus." This text explains the background of the stone carving's location and discovery. The video then returns to the initial painting, with additional text appearing at the bottom of the screen: "The ancient legends of many nations mention dragons. If you go into detail, these mythical creatures are very similar to dinosaurs. In other words, dragon is the folkloric name for a dinosaur. How could these ancient animals get into myths and legends if, according to the generally accepted scientific theory, dinosaurs became extinct tens of millions of years before the appearance of man?"
